extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians in arithmetic geometry and Inter-universal Teichmüller (IUT) theory
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive/technical guidance for performing Hodge–Arakelov/theta evaluations and constructing Gaussian (M-theoretic) theta monoids in the IUT framework, including choices of base points/subgraphs, cyclotomic rigidity isomorphisms, and functoriality requirements for evaluation algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Galois evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'mysterious evaluation algorithm' which constructs theta values from an abstract theta function should be compatible with taking Kummer classes of the abstract theta function and the theta values, should extend to coverings on both input and output data, and should be functorial with respect to the Galois groups on either side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If these natural requirements hold, the evaluation algorithm arises from a section G → (5)(127)Y((5)) of the natural surjection (5)(127)Y((5)) → G (Proposition 11.10). From the viewpoint of the global Conjecture one expects these sections to arise from geometric points. Anti-pattern: using an evaluation algorithm that is not compatible with Kummer classes or not functorial for Galois action, since then it will not descend to the required group-theoretic section and will not satisfy the Galois-evaluation principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a single base point for theta evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform the evaluation algorithm using a single base point (i.e., a connected subgraph (0)I ⊂ (0)(127)Y) so that theta values live in the cohomology of a single Galois group Gv((5)v(127)I) with a single cyclotomic coefficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures the collection of theta values (for various labels jtj ∈ |Fl|) can be treated as a 'connected single object' rather than separated objects; indeterminacies are synchronised via Fo6-symmetry when constructing Gaussian monoids (cf. Corollary 11.17). Anti-pattern: evaluating with multiple base points (disconnected choices), which leaves unsynchronised indeterminacies and prevents treating theta values as a coherent object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose finite subgraph: connectedness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purpose of obtaining a single base point, the chosen finite subgraph (0)0 must be connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This connectedness is required so the evaluation uses a single base point / single connected subgraph as explained in Remark 11.10.2. Anti-pattern: selecting a disconnected subgraph which would produce multiple base points and violate the single-base-point requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose finite subgraph: include vertex labelled 0
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purpose of obtaining the crucial splitting in Proposition 11.10(4), the chosen finite subgraph (0)0 should contain the vertex of label 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including the vertex labelled 0 is necessary to obtain the splittings used later in the construction. Anti-pattern: omitting the label-0 vertex and losing the required splitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose finite subgraph: maximize the height-sharpness function
rubrics_metrics.description: To make the final height inequality sharpest (cf. calculations in the proof of Lemma 1.10), one should choose (0)0 to maximise the value min_{j∈(0)0} |j| in |Fl| averaged as prescribed (equivalently grow #(0)0 until the objective function stabilises).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically this means taking #(0)0 large (the text indicates one obtains #(0)0 ≥ l> and the function is non-decreasing with #(0)0). This choice is motivated by optimizing the final height inequality. Anti-pattern: choosing too small a subgraph and thereby weakening the height inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose finite subgraph: uniqueness per label for globalisation/product formula
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purpose of globalising the monoids determined by theta values via global realised Frobenioids so that the product formula is satisfied, the set { j ∈ (0)0 ; |j| ∈ |Fl| } should consist of exactly one element for each j ∈ F>l.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If this set has more than one element, independent conjugacy indeterminacies (described in Remark 11.10.3) are incompatible with the product formula. The combination of the four conditions (connectedness, contains label 0, maximise function, uniqueness per label) forces the only admissible subgraph to be (0)I(127)Y. Anti-pattern: allowing multiple representatives per label, which prevents satisfying the product formula when globalising monoids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cyclotomic-rigidity isomorphisms appropriately (trade-offs)
rubrics_metrics.description: One may use the cyclotomic-rigidity isomorphism via positive rational structure and local class field theory (LCFT) as an alternative route to obtain the cyclotomic identifications; this approach yields a natural surjection used in Corollary 3.19 and can construct some constant monoids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method has the advantage of a natural surjection H^1(Gv((0)); (22)bZ(Gv((0)))) → bZ used to build constant monoids, but the resulting algorithm is only uniradially defined (unlike constructions based on full mono-theta cyclotomic rigidity). One must therefore be aware of the trade-off between having the natural surjection (helpful to build constants) and losing multiradial/full functorial definition. Anti-pattern: assuming both full multiradial definition and the LCFT-surjection advantages without accounting for the uniradial limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label consistency and ambient 'container' for conjugacy classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the global data (1)}(6) (= b(1)(6)_v) as an 'ambient container' for b(1)(6)_v-conjugates of cuspidal inertia subgroups It and (1)v(127)I, so that (6)-labels on local objects are defined consistently in the form of conjugacy classes of It.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When varying the place v, the topological group (5)_v(127)I is purely local and cannot be globalised; hence one must account for independent conjugacy indeterminacies when varying v. These independent indeterminacies are the reason the label container is needed and why naive globalisation of local groups fails. Anti-pattern: treating local topological groups as globalisable objects and ignoring the conjugacy indeterminacies that obstruct the product formula/global constructions.
